page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.u1-c1m2.large is a dual-vCPU entry-tier instance within the universal general-purpose u1 series, operating on KVM virtualization. The instance provisions 2 vCPUs derived from 1 physical Intel Xeon core running at 2.5 GHz with hyperthreading enabled, paired with 4.0 GB of system memory (2.0 GB per vCPU). Hardware instruction support includes AVX, AVX-512F, AES, and FMA. It includes no bundled local storage and no GPU accelerators, routing disk operations entirely to network-attached block volumes. Baseline network throughput is rated at 1 Gbps with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Benchmark results demonstrate modest computational capability constrained by its single underlying physical core. The instance attains average single-thread performance, posting a Geekbench single-core score of 1358.0 and a stress-ng single-core score of 1833.19, with steady single-threaded gzip compression at 27.52 GB/sec. However, multi-threaded metrics rank in the bottom 10 percent of recorded systems, yielding a Geekbench multi-core score of 1584.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 2706.57. Memory throughput reaches 14.29 GB/sec for uncached 256 MB reads and 12.87 GB/sec for writes, contributing to lower comparative throughput across database operations (PassMark database score of 1002.31) and Redis operations (1.9 million SET ops/sec).

From an infrastructure cost efficiency standpoint, the ecs.u1-c1m2.large provides a low operational cost footprint for low-intensity baseline services where dedicated high-throughput multi-core execution is unnecessary. It is functionally aligned with lightweight utility tasks, development and test staging environments, basic reverse proxies, small internal microservices, and modest web serving workloads.

Tradeoffs include limited total memory headroom, lack of bundled local NVMe storage, and diminished multi-core scaling due to hyperthread sharing on a single core. Workloads involving continuous high-concurrency computation, heavy database transactions, large-scale caching arrays, or local IOPS-intensive applications should deploy larger multi-core instance classes.
